name: The spoked-wheel chariot
summary: Herders of the Ural steppe build light chariots on spoked wheels, drawn by horses.
changed: Within a few centuries chariots run from Egypt to the Shang court. Armies and envoys cross far more ground, and the known worlds of Babylon, Egypt and China all widen.

name: The outrigger canoe
summary: Austronesian boatbuilders lash a float to a dugout hull on outrigger booms, making a narrow canoe stable in open water.
changed: Sailors cross from island to island and eventually reach Madagascar in one direction and Easter Island in the other: the widest spread of any people before 1500.

name: The Turin papyrus map
summary: The scribe Amennakhte draws the Wadi Hammamat for an expedition to its quarries, with roads, hills coloured by rock and the gold mines marked.
changed: The oldest surviving map of a real place drawn to be used on the ground.

name: Writing on oracle bones
summary: Shang diviners carve questions and answers into turtle shell and ox bone: the earliest Chinese writing to survive.
changed: The first written record of the lands around China: the fang the Shang fought, traded with and feared.

name: The Phoenician alphabet
summary: Phoenician scribes write with twenty-two letters for consonants alone, simple enough for merchants to learn.
changed: Carried by Tyre's ships across the Mediterranean, it becomes the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts in which most of the world's journeys were later written.

name: Wayfinding by stars and swells
summary: Navigators steer by the rising and setting points of stars, read ocean swells through the hull and watch birds and clouds for land, all held in memory, not on paper.
changed: Lets canoes find islands across thousands of kilometres of open ocean, and later settle the whole Polynesian Triangle.

name: The domesticated camel
summary: Camels, herded in Arabia for milk and meat, are now ridden and loaded for long desert crossings.
changed: The incense road from Saba to Gaza opens, and later the routes across the Sahara.

name: The Babylonian Map of the World
summary: A clay tablet shows Babylon on the Euphrates inside a ring of 'bitter river', with far islands beyond where the sun is never seen.
changed: The oldest surviving map of the whole world as one people imagined it.

name: The Royal Road and its relay riders
summary: Darius's road runs some 2,500 km from Sardis to Susa, with a hundred and eleven staging posts, each holding fresh horses and riders for the king's messages.
changed: A message that took three months on foot crosses the empire in about a week. Herodotus's account of the road gave the Greeks their picture of the Persian interior.

name: The spherical Earth
summary: Aristotle argues the Earth is a sphere: the curved shadow it casts on the Moon in an eclipse, and stars that rise or vanish as a traveller goes north or south.
changed: Once the Earth is a ball it has a size to measure and a known world that is only part of it: the question every later map tries to answer.

name: The Library of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemies gather every book they can find, copying the scrolls of ships in the harbour, into a library beside the Museum.
changed: Eratosthenes, Hipparchus and Ptolemy work from its collections; the travellers' reports of three continents are brought into one place and one language.

name: The lighthouse of Alexandria
summary: On the island of Pharos the Ptolemies raise a tower more than a hundred metres high, with a fire at its top that ships can see far out on a low, featureless coast.
changed: Ships make the Mediterranean's greatest port by night as well as by day. Pharos becomes the word for a lighthouse in Greek and Latin and the languages that came from them.

name: Measuring the Earth
summary: Eratosthenes compares the Sun's angle at noon in Alexandria and Syene and works out the Earth's circumference to within a few percent.
changed: Gives the known world a scale: how much of the globe it actually covers.

name: Sailing on the monsoon
summary: Greek pilots from Egypt learn what Arab and Indian sailors knew: the summer wind blows steadily from the southwest, the winter wind back again.
changed: Ships cross the open Arabian Sea to India in weeks instead of hugging the coast; by Strabo's day 120 ships a year sail for India from Egypt.

name: The sternpost rudder
summary: Han shipwrights hang a rudder on the centre of the stern, as a pottery ship model from a Guangzhou tomb shows.
changed: Large ships can be steered in heavy seas; with the compass and the junk it makes the long Chinese voyages of the Song and Ming possible.

name: Sewn-plank boats
summary: Boatbuilders of the East African coast stitch planks together with coconut-fibre cord instead of nails. The Periplus says the market town of Rhapta was named for its sewn boats.
changed: The hulls flex with the ocean swell and can be mended with what grows on shore. Sewn mtepe ships carried the coast's trade for almost two thousand years.

name: Paper
summary: Cai Lun reports a method of making paper from bark, hemp and rags to the Han court.
changed: Cheap writing material lets reports and maps travel and survive; it reaches Baghdad by about 800 and Europe by about 1100.

name: Coordinates of latitude and longitude
summary: Ptolemy's Geography lists some 8,000 places by latitude and longitude, so that a map can be redrawn by anyone from the numbers alone.
changed: Maps become reproducible data rather than one-off pictures.

name: Pei Xiu's six principles of map-making
summary: Pei Xiu sets out scale, a rectangular grid, true distances and corrections for height and bends in roads.
changed: Chinese maps are drawn on measured grids for the next fifteen centuries.

name: The Roman road map
summary: A long roll draws the empire's roads from Britain to India as one strip, with distances between stations: the map we know as the Tabula Peutingeriana.
changed: A traveller could plan a journey stage by stage across the known world; it is the map of a road network, not of the shape of the land.

name: The lateen sail
summary: A triangular sail set on a long slanting yard, the rig of the dhows of the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.
changed: Ships sail closer to the wind; the dhow carries the trade of the monsoon ocean for fifteen centuries, and the lateen later goes into the caravel.

name: Place-value numerals with zero
summary: Brahmagupta sets out rules for calculating with zero in a place-value system of nine digits and a sign for nothing.
changed: Through Baghdad and al-Khwarizmi the numerals reach the whole Islamic world and then Europe: the arithmetic behind every astronomical table, latitude and survey.

name: The astrolabe in the Islamic world
summary: Astronomers of Abbasid Baghdad build and refine the astrolabe, a brass model of the sky for telling time and measuring the height of stars.
changed: Latitudes measured by observation; the direction and distance of Mecca from any city; better maps.

name: The Viking longship
summary: A long, light, clinker-built ship with a keel and a square sail, shallow enough to row up rivers and strong enough for the open Atlantic.
changed: The Norse reach Constantinople by river, Iceland and Greenland by sea, and North America by 1000.

name: Measuring the Earth from a mountain
summary: Al-Biruni climbs a hill above the Punjab plain, measures the dip of the horizon and works out the Earth's radius.
changed: A single observer can measure the globe without a long journey; his figure is within about one per cent of the true one.

name: Movable type
summary: Bi Sheng prints with individual characters of baked clay, as recorded by Shen Kuo.
changed: Printing lets geographic works like Zhao Rugua's spread in many copies.

name: The magnetic compass
summary: Shen Kuo describes a magnetized needle and notes that it points a little east of true south; by 1119 Zhu Yu reports pilots using it at sea in overcast weather.
changed: Ships can hold a course out of sight of land and under cloud. It is in use in the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean by about 1200.

name: The dog sledge and the umiak
summary: Thule hunters harness teams of dogs to sledges and build open skin boats large enough for a whole family and a whale hunt.
changed: In a few generations they cross the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland, the fastest migration of any people over such a distance.

name: The double-hulled voyaging canoe
summary: Two hulls lashed side by side under one deck and crab-claw sails carry dozens of people, with pigs, dogs and chickens and the plants for a new garden.
changed: Within two or three centuries settlers reach Hawaii, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa, the last large lands on Earth to be settled.

name: A gridded map in stone
summary: The Map of the Tracks of Yu is carved on a stele on a grid of squares a hundred li across, with rivers and coasts strikingly accurate.
changed: Maps can be copied exactly by rubbing and enlarged square by square; Chinese cartography keeps the grid for centuries.

name: The kamal
summary: A wooden card on a knotted string: held at arm's length against the Pole Star, the knot shows the ship's latitude.
changed: Pilots of the Indian Ocean sail along a parallel to a known port; Ibn Majid's rutters give the star altitudes of every harbour.

name: The ocean-going junk
summary: Song shipyards build large seagoing junks with watertight bulkheads, several masts and battened sails.
changed: Chinese merchants sail regularly to Southeast Asia, India and beyond; the junk carries Zheng He's fleets two centuries later.

name: Al-Idrisi's world map
summary: At the court of Roger II of Sicily, al-Idrisi combines Arabic geography with the reports of travellers questioned at the port into seventy sectional maps and a silver planisphere.
changed: The most complete picture of Eurasia and North Africa of its century, copied in the Islamic world for three hundred years.

name: The Mongol post
summary: Ögedei Khan sets up relay stations a day's ride apart across the empire, with fresh horses and food for anyone carrying the khan's pass, the paiza.
changed: Orders and envoys cross from China to the Volga in weeks. Carpini, Rubruck and the Polos travelled its post roads and brought Europe its first eyewitness picture of East Asia.

name: The Mamluk post and its pigeons
summary: Sultan Baybars rebuilds the barid, the state post, with relays of horses and lofts of carrier pigeons flying messages between Cairo, Damascus and the frontier.
changed: News from the Euphrates frontier reaches the citadel of Cairo within days. The post's routes and stations were written up in Mamluk chancery manuals, among the fullest road books of their age.

name: Portolan charts
summary: Sea charts drawn from compass bearings and sailing distances, criss-crossed by rhumb lines; the Carta Pisana is the oldest to survive.
changed: Coasts drawn with a new accuracy, and a chart that pilots trust over written sailing directions.

name: The Catalan Atlas
summary: Abraham Cresques's workshop paints a world map on vellum panels, joining the portolan coasts with Marco Polo's Asia and Mansa Musa holding his gold.
changed: The finest world picture of its day, given as a royal gift; it shows Europe what lay along the caravan and spice routes.

name: The Kangnido map
native: 混一疆理歷代國都之圖
summary: Korean scholars combine Chinese maps of the Mongol era with their own and Japan's into one map of the world from Korea to Europe and Africa.
changed: Africa's southern tip appears on it decades before any Portuguese ship rounded the Cape.

name: Ptolemy's Geography in Latin
summary: In Florence, Jacopo Angeli finishes a Latin translation of Ptolemy's Geography, a book the Greek scholar Manuel Chrysoloras had brought from Constantinople.
changed: Western Europe recovers a world laid out by latitude and longitude. Printed with maps from 1477, Ptolemy became the frame the new discoveries were fitted into, and then broke.

name: Zheng He's sailing charts
summary: The pilots of the treasure fleets set down their routes from Nanjing to Hormuz and East Africa as one long strip of coast, with compass bearings, hours of sailing and the heights of stars for each crossing.
changed: Chinese knowledge of the Indian Ocean is written down rather than kept in pilots' heads. The chart survives because it was printed in the military encyclopedia Wubei zhi in 1621.

name: The caravel
summary: A small, light ship with lateen sails that can beat into the wind.
changed: Ships can return north against the trade winds, which opens the African coast and the open Atlantic.

name: The printing press
summary: Gutenberg combines metal type, oil-based ink and a press.
changed: Ptolemy is printed with maps in 1477; Columbus's letter of 1493 is reprinted across Europe within months. News of discoveries now spreads in copies by the thousand.

name: Khipu, the knotted record
summary: Cords of coloured cotton, knotted in a decimal code, record census counts, tribute and perhaps narratives; specialists read them aloud.
changed: The Inca run an empire of ten million people across the Andes without writing, and know its every valley's population.

name: Painted maps of the Valley of Mexico
summary: Painters draw land and history together on bark paper and cloth: footprints for journeys, glyphs for towns, rivers and lakes around them.
changed: Communities record their territory and migrations; Spanish officials later depend on these maps for the Relaciones Geográficas.

name: The Inca road
summary: Some 40,000 kilometres of roads, with stairways, suspension bridges and waystations a day apart, run from Ecuador to Chile.
changed: Relay runners carry messages 250 kilometres a day; the whole of the Andes is held in one view from Cusco.

name: The chasqui relay runners
summary: Runners wait in pairs at posts a few kilometres apart along the royal roads, passing on spoken messages and knotted khipu at a run.
changed: A message covers some 240 km a day; the Sapa Inca in Cusco hears from Quito, 2,000 km away, in about a week.

name: Behaim's globe
summary: Martin Behaim and the painter Georg Glockendon make a globe for the city council of Nuremberg, drawn from Ptolemy, Marco Polo and Portuguese charts. It is the oldest globe that survives.
changed: The world can be turned in the hand. It has no Americas, and the ocean between Portugal and Cipangu is only a little wider than Columbus hoped; he sailed the same year.

name: The map that named America
summary: Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann print a twelve-sheet map of the world that shows a separate New World and names it America, after Amerigo Vespucci.
changed: The idea that Columbus had reached not Asia but a fourth part of the world went into print, in a thousand copies, with the name that stuck.

name: The Piri Reis map
summary: The Ottoman captain Piri Reis compiles a map of the world from about twenty sources, among them, he writes, a chart drawn by Columbus himself.
changed: The surviving piece shows the Atlantic coasts of Africa and Iberia and the new lands of the Caribbean and Brazil: news of the discoveries had crossed the Mediterranean within twenty years.

name: The Mercator projection
summary: Gerardus Mercator draws the world so that any line of constant compass bearing is straight.
changed: A navigator can lay a ruler on the chart and steer by it. (The flat map in this atlas uses the same projection.)

name: The first modern atlas
summary: Abraham Ortelius gathers maps of every region, drawn to one style and bound in one book, with a list of the cartographers he used.
changed: The world becomes a book anyone with money could buy, revised edition by edition as new coasts were reached.

name: The backstaff
summary: John Davis's quadrant measures the Sun's height by the shadow it casts, with the navigator's back to the Sun.
changed: Latitude can be taken without looking into the Sun, more precisely than with the cross-staff; it stays in use until the octant.

name: Ricci's map of the world
summary: The Jesuit Matteo Ricci and the scholar Li Zhizao print a great map of the world in Chinese, with China near the centre and the continents and seas of the European map named in Chinese.
changed: Chinese readers see the Americas and a round earth drawn for the first time. Names it coined, such as 亚细亚 for Asia, are still in use, and copies reached Japan and Korea.

name: The telescope
summary: Hans Lipperhey applies for a patent on a spyglass; Galileo turns one to the sky the next year.
changed: Timing the moons of Jupiter gives the first accurate way to fix longitude on land.

name: Triangulation
summary: Willebrord Snellius measures a long distance by a chain of triangles from one measured baseline.
changed: The method behind the Kangxi atlas, the Cassini map of France and the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India: the 'surveyed' level of this map.

name: The octant and sextant
summary: John Hadley shows the Royal Society an instrument whose two mirrors let a navigator hold a star against the horizon while the ship rolls beneath him.
changed: Latitude comes to within a few minutes of arc. Enlarged into the sextant, it measures the lunar distances that, with the chronometer, give longitude as well.

name: The Cihannüma, printed in Istanbul
summary: İbrahim Müteferrika, founder of the first Ottoman Turkish press, prints Kâtip Çelebi's geography of the world, the Cihannüma, with maps engraved in Istanbul.
changed: Ottoman readers get a printed geography that joins Islamic learning to the European atlases of Mercator and Blaeu.

name: The marine chronometer
summary: John Harrison's H4 keeps time at sea to within seconds a day on a voyage to Jamaica.
changed: Longitude at sea, at last. Cook carries a copy on his second voyage and charts the Pacific with it.

name: The Cassini map of France
summary: César-François Cassini de Thury begins to map the whole of France on a network of measured triangles, in 182 sheets at about 1:86,400; his son finishes it.
changed: The first map of a whole country drawn from a full survey, at a single scale. Every national survey that followed across Europe took it as the model.

name: The hot-air balloon
summary: The Montgolfier brothers' balloon carries the first people into the air.
changed: The first view of the land from above; balloon photographs follow in 1858.

name: The semaphore telegraph
summary: Claude Chappe's line of towers with movable arms carries signals from Paris to Lille. Its first great message, news of a victory at the frontier, arrives within the hour.
changed: A government can hear from its frontiers the same day. By the 1840s France had more than five hundred stations, and lines ran across Europe.

name: The Great Trigonometrical Survey
summary: William Lambton measures a baseline near Madras and begins to cover India with chains of triangles, a survey carried on by George Everest.
changed: Over seventy years it fixes the shape of the subcontinent and measures the Himalaya. In 1852 its computers found Peak XV to be the highest mountain on Earth.

name: Ino Tadataka's survey of Japan
summary: A retired merchant walks Japan's coasts for seventeen years, measuring by pacing, rope and stars, and his team finishes the map after his death.
changed: Japan's outline is fixed with modern accuracy; the map so impresses the British in 1861 that they abandon their own survey of the coast.

name: The railway
summary: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens: steam locomotives pulling passengers and goods on a schedule.
changed: Interiors open up: within decades rails cross North America, India and Russia, and a continent can be crossed in a week.

name: Charts of sticks and shells
summary: Marshallese navigators tie palm ribs and shells into frames that show how ocean swells bend and cross around islands.
changed: Studied ashore and memorised, not carried at sea: a way of seeing the ocean as patterns of waves that no other mapping tradition shared.

name: Steamships across the ocean
summary: The Great Western crosses from Bristol to New York in fifteen days under steam, on a regular service.
changed: Voyages keep timetables rather than winds; steamers push up the Niger, the Congo and the Yangzi, and the world's coasts draw closer.

name: Photography
summary: Daguerre's process is made public by the French Academy of Sciences.
changed: Expeditions bring back pictures rather than drawings; distant places become visible at home.

name: The electric telegraph
summary: Samuel Morse sends "What hath God wrought" along a wire from Washington to Baltimore, in a code of dots and dashes.
changed: For the first time news travels faster than any rider, ship or train. Within a decade wires join most American and European cities, and newspapers, markets and railways run on them.

name: The Illustrated Treatise on the Sea Kingdoms
summary: After China's defeat in the Opium War, Wei Yuan compiles an account of the countries of the world, with maps of every continent, from the translations of Western books gathered by Lin Zexu.
changed: The fullest account of the outside world yet written in Chinese. It was read even more eagerly in Japan, where it fed the debate over opening the country.

name: The transatlantic telegraph
summary: A lasting cable between Ireland and Newfoundland carries messages in minutes rather than weeks.
changed: The gap between when a traveller sees something and when home knows it shrinks almost to nothing; Amundsen's news goes round the world from Hobart by cable.

name: The telephone
summary: Alexander Graham Bell patents the telephone and, in his Boston workshop, calls his assistant Thomas Watson down the wire.
changed: A voice carries across a city, and by 1915 across the continent. Talking no longer needs people to be in the same place.

name: Carved wooden maps
summary: Kunit carves pieces of driftwood whose bumps and notches follow the coast of East Greenland, fjord by fjord.
changed: Maps to be read by touch, in a kayak and in the dark, and that float if dropped; they show the coast as a traveller meets it.

name: The ocean icebreaker
summary: Admiral Makarov's Yermak, the first icebreaker built to work in the open polar sea, reaches Kronstadt.
changed: Ships can force a way through Arctic ice; the Northern Sea Route along Siberia becomes a working seaway in the 1930s.

name: Radio across the ocean
summary: Guglielmo Marconi's station in Cornwall sends the letter S in Morse across the Atlantic to Newfoundland, with no wire.
changed: Ships at sea and expeditions in the field can report at once; the gap between seeing a place and home knowing it closes.

name: Powered flight
summary: The Wright brothers fly a powered aircraft for twelve seconds.
changed: Aerial survey: by the 1950s photographs from aircraft map whole continents, including New Guinea's highlands and the Amazon.

name: Echo sounding
summary: Reginald Fessenden's oscillator sends sound to the sea floor and times the echo; the German Meteor expedition of 1925–27 makes 67,000 soundings with it.
changed: Depths measured in seconds instead of hours with a weighted line; the way to Tharp and Heezen's map of the ocean floor.

name: Radar
summary: Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins show that a bomber flying near Daventry reflects a BBC shortwave signal strongly enough to be detected.
changed: Ships and aircraft can see through darkness and cloud. After the war radar guides airliners and maps storms, and later charts the ice beneath Antarctica and the surface of Venus.

name: Radiocarbon dating
summary: Willard Libby shows that the decay of carbon-14 can date bones, wood and charcoal.
changed: Most of the Humanity layer's dates, and Polynesia's, come from this method and its successors.

name: The jet airliner
summary: Jet airliners enter service across the Atlantic and the Pacific, flying above the weather at 900 kilometres an hour.
changed: Any city is a day from any other; ordinary travellers see continents their grandparents knew only from books.

name: Earth-observing satellites
summary: Landsat 1 begins photographing the whole land surface every 18 days. The same year Apollo 17's crew photographs the whole Earth.
changed: No land surface is unmapped; the remaining fog is under ice and water.

name: Satellite positioning (GPS)
summary: A constellation of satellites lets a receiver fix its position anywhere to within metres; it is fully operational from 1995.
changed: Anyone can know exactly where they are, with no stars, chronometer or survey.

name: The World Wide Web
summary: Tim Berners-Lee at CERN publishes the first website: documents linked across the internet that anyone can read and write.
changed: Maps, pictures and reports of every place are a click away for everyone; knowing the world stops depending on where you stand.
